claim: Synchronous neurotransmitter release is triggered by Ca2+ binding to the synaptic vesicle protein Synaptotagmin 1.
source: Synchronous neurotransmitter release is triggered by Ca2+ binding to the synaptic vesicle protein Synaptotagmin 1, while asynchronous fusion and short-term facilitation is hypothesized to be mediated by plasma membrane-localized Synaptotagmin 7 (SYT7).
evidence: This is a well-established finding in the field, supported by citations in the introduction and consistent with the literature on SYT1 function.

claim: Asynchronous fusion and short-term facilitation is hypothesized to be mediated by plasma membrane-localized Synaptotagmin 7 (SYT7).
source: Synchronous neurotransmitter release is triggered by Ca2+ binding to the synaptic vesicle protein Synaptotagmin 1, while asynchronous fusion and short-term facilitation is hypothesized to be mediated by plasma membrane-localized Synaptotagmin 7 (SYT7).
evidence: This is a hypothesis being tested in the manuscript, supported by prior literature citations.

claim: Evoked release was elevated 2-fold in Syt7 mutants.
source: Electrophysiology and quantal imaging revealed evoked release was elevated 2-fold.
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiology data presented in Figure 2 showing increased eEJC amplitude in Syt7M1 mutants.

claim: Syt7 mutants had a larger pool of readily-releasable vesicles.
source: Syt7 mutants also had a larger pool of readily-releasable vesicles, faster recovery following stimulation, and intact facilitation.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 9 showing increased cumulative quanta released during high frequency stimulation.

claim: Syt7 mutants had faster recovery following stimulation.
source: Syt7 mutants also had a larger pool of readily-releasable vesicles, faster recovery following stimulation, and intact facilitation.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 10 showing enhanced P531/P530 ratio in Syt7M1 mutants.

claim: Syt7 mutants had intact facilitation.
source: Syt7 mutants also had a larger pool of readily-releasable vesicles, faster recovery following stimulation, and intact facilitation.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 8 showing paired-pulse facilitation in Syt7M1 mutants.

claim: Syt1/Syt7 double mutants displayed more release than Syt1 mutants alone.
source: Syt1/Syt7 double mutants displayed more release than Syt1 mutants alone, indicating SYT7 does not mediate the residual asynchronous release remaining in the absence of SYT1.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data in Figure 7 showing increased eEJC amplitude and charge in DoubleNull compared to Syt1Null.

claim: SYT7 does not mediate the residual asynchronous release remaining in the absence of SYT1.
source: Syt1/Syt7 double mutants displayed more release than Syt1 mutants alone, indicating SYT7 does not mediate the residual asynchronous release remaining in the absence of SYT1.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that double mutants have more release than Syt1 mutants alone.

claim: SYT7 localizes to an internal membrane tubular network within the peri-active zone.
source: SYT7 localizes to an internal membrane tubular network within the peri-active zone, but does not enrich at active zones.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data in Figures 11 and 12 showing SYT7RFP localization pattern.

claim: SYT7 does not enrich at active zones.
source: SYT7 localizes to an internal membrane tubular network within the peri-active zone, but does not enrich at active zones.
evidence: This is supported by co-localization analysis in Figure 12 showing low Pearson correlation between SYT7 and BRP (r = -0.11).

claim: The two Ca2+ sensor model of SYT1 and SYT7 mediating all phases of neurotransmitter release and facilitation is not applicable at Drosophila synapses.
source: These findings indicate the two Ca2+ sensor model of SYT1 and SYT7 mediating all phases of neurotransmitter release and facilitation is not applicable at Drosophila synapses.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental findings including double mutant analysis and facilitation assays.

claim: Neurotransmitter release from presynaptic terminals is the primary mechanism of synaptic communication.
source: Neurotransmitter release from presynaptic terminals is the primary mechanism of synaptic communication and is mediated by fusion of synaptic vesicles (SVs) with the plasma membrane at specific sites known as active zones (AZs) (Katz, 1969; Südhof, 2013; Zhai and Bellen, 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by citations.

claim: Neurotransmitter release is mediated by fusion of synaptic vesicles (SVs) with the plasma membrane at specific sites known as active zones (AZs).
source: Neurotransmitter release from presynaptic terminals is the primary mechanism of synaptic communication and is mediated by fusion of synaptic vesicles (SVs) with the plasma membrane at specific sites known as active zones (AZs) (Katz, 1969; Südhof, 2013; Zhai and Bellen, 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by citations.

claim: A highly conserved protein machinery composed of the SNARE complex drives fusion between the SV and AZ lipid bilayers.
source: A highly conserved protein machinery composed of the SNARE complex drives fusion between the SV and AZ lipid bilayers (Littleton et al., 1998; Söllner et al., 1993; Sutton et al., 1998; Tucker et al., 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by citations.

claim: Ca2+ influx through voltage-gated Ca2+ channels functions as the trigger to activate the fusion process.
source: Ca2+ influx through voltage-gated Ca2+ channels functions as the trigger to activate the fusion process (Borst and Sakmann, 1996; Katz and Miledi, 1970; Katz and Miledi, 1967; Schneggenburger and Rosenmund, 2015; Südhof, 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by citations.

claim: The majority of SVs fuse during a synchronous phase that occurs within a few milliseconds of Ca2+ entry.
source: The majority of SVs fuse during a synchronous phase that occurs within a few milliseconds of Ca2+ entry (Borst and Sakmann, 1996; Goda and Stevens, 1994; Llinás et al., 1981; Sabatini and Regehr, 1996; Yoshihara and Littleton, 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by citations.

claim: Many synapses have an asynchronous component that results in SV release over hundreds of milliseconds.
source: Many synapses also have an asynchronous component that results in SV release over hundreds of milliseconds (Goda and Stevens, 1994; Hefft and Jonas, 2005; Kaeser and Regehr, 2014; Yoshihara and Littleton, 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by citations.

claim: Asynchronous release normally accounts for less than 5% of SV fusion following single action potentials at Drosophila neuromuscular junctions (NMJs).
source: Asynchronous release normally accounts for less than 5% of SV fusion following single action potentials at Drosophila neuromuscular junctions (NMJs) (Jorquera et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The slower phase of release becomes more prominent during high rates of stimulation.
source: This slower phase of release becomes more prominent during high rates of stimulation (Atluri and Regehr, 1998; Lu and Trussell, 2000; Rozov et al., 2019; Zucker and Regehr, 2002) and mediates all SV fusion at some neuronal connections (Best and Regehr, 2009; Peters et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by citations.

claim: Asynchronous release mediates all SV fusion at some neuronal connections.
source: This slower phase of release becomes more prominent during high rates of stimulation (Atluri and Regehr, 1998; Lu and Trussell, 2000; Rozov et al., 2019; Zucker and Regehr, 2002) and mediates all SV fusion at some neuronal connections (Best and Regehr, 2009; Peters et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by citations.

claim: The Synaptotagmin (SYT) family of Ca2+ binding proteins contain key regulators that control the timing of SV release.
source: The Synaptotagmin (SYT) family of Ca2+ binding proteins contain key regulators that control the timing of SV release.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by extensive literature on SYT proteins.

claim: SYT proteins have a transmembrane domain and two Ca2+ binding C2 domains termed C2A and C2B.
source: SYT proteins have a transmembrane domain and two Ca2+ binding C2 domains termed C2A and C2B (Adolfsen et al., 2004; Adolfsen and Littleton, 2001; Perin et al., 1990; Sugita et al., 2002; Ullrich and Südhof, 1995).
evidence: This is established knowledge about SYT protein structure, supported by citations.

claim: Mammals have three SYT family members that localize to SVs (SYT1, SYT2 and SYT9).
source: Mammals have three SYT family members that localize to SVs (SYT1, SYT2 and SYT9), while Drosophila contains a single member of the SV subfamily (SYT1) (Littleton et al., 1993a; Pang et al., 2006; Xu et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge about SYT family members, supported by citations.

claim: Drosophila contains a single member of the SV subfamily (SYT1).
source: Mammals have three SYT family members that localize to SVs (SYT1, SYT2 and SYT9), while Drosophila contains a single member of the SV subfamily (SYT1) (Littleton et al., 1993a; Pang et al., 2006; Xu et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Drosophila SYT proteins, supported by citations.

claim: SYT isoforms bind Ca2+ and activate synchronous fusion of SVs via interactions with membranes and the SNARE complex.
source: These SYT isoforms bind Ca2+ and activate synchronous fusion of SVs via interactions with membranes and the SNARE complex (Chang et al., 2018; Chapman and Jahn, 1994; Fernández-Chacón et al., 2001; Geppert et al., 1994; Guan et al., 2017; Lee et al., 2013; Lee and Littleton, 2015; Littleton et al., 1994; Littleton et al., 1993b; Mackler et al., 2002; Nishiki and Augustine, 2004; Tucker et al., 2004; Xu et al., 2007; Yoshihara and Littleton, 2002; Young and Neher, 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge about SYT1 function, supported by extensive citations.

claim: SYT7 is the only other family member implicated in Ca2+-dependent SV trafficking beyond SV localized SYTs.
source: Beyond SV localized SYTs, SYT7 is the only other family member implicated in Ca2+-dependent SV trafficking, although additional SYT isoforms participate in Ca2+-dependent fusion of other secretory organelles and dense core vesicles (DCVs) (Adolfsen et al., 2004; Cao et al., 2011; Dean et al., 2012; Li et al., 1995; Moghadam and Jackson, 2013; Park et al., 2014; Shin et al., 2002; Yoshihara et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on SYT7 function.

claim: Additional SYT isoforms participate in Ca2+-dependent fusion of other secretory organelles and dense core vesicles (DCVs).
source: Beyond SV localized SYTs, SYT7 is the only other family member implicated in Ca2+-dependent SV trafficking, although additional SYT isoforms participate in Ca2+-dependent fusion of other secretory organelles and dense core vesicles (DCVs) (Adolfsen et al., 2004; Cao et al., 2011; Dean et al., 2012; Li et al., 1995; Moghadam and Jackson, 2013; Park et al., 2014; Shin et al., 2002; Yoshihara et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge about other SYT isoforms, supported by citations.

claim: Syt1 mutants have enhanced asynchronous release.
source: Although several mechanisms may contribute, the observation that Syt1 mutants have enhanced asynchronous release indicates another Ca2+ sensor(s) activates the remaining slower Ca2+-dependent component of exocytosis (Huson et al., 2019; Kochubey and Schneggenburger, 2011; Nishiki and Augustine, 2004; Turecek and Regehr, 2019; Yang et al., 2010; Yoshihara et al., 2010; Yoshihara and Littleton, 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior studies, supported by citations.

claim: Another Ca2+ sensor(s) activates the remaining slower Ca2+-dependent component of exocytosis in Syt1 mutants.
source: Although several mechanisms may contribute, the observation that Syt1 mutants have enhanced asynchronous release indicates another Ca2+ sensor(s) activates the remaining slower Ca2+-dependent component of exocytosis (Huson et al., 2019; Kochubey and Schneggenburger, 2011; Nishiki and Augustine, 2004; Turecek and Regehr, 2019; Yang et al., 2010; Yoshihara et al., 2010; Yoshihara and Littleton, 2002).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from observations in Syt1 mutants, supported by citations.

claim: SYT7 has emerged as a popular candidate for the asynchronous Ca2+ sensor.
source: SYT7 has emerged as a popular candidate for the asynchronous Ca2+ sensor (Bacaj et al., 2013; Chen et al., 2017; Maximov et al., 2008; Turecek and Regehr, 2019; Turecek and Regehr, 2018; Weber et al., 2014; Wen et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature proposing SYT7 as an asynchronous sensor.

claim: SYT7 has been postulated to function as the Ca2+ sensor for short-term synaptic facilitation.
source: SYT7 has also been postulated to function as the Ca2+ sensor for short-term synaptic facilitation (Chen et al., 2017; Jackman et al., 2016; Turecek and Regehr, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature proposing SYT7 as a facilitation sensor.

claim: SYT7 has higher Ca2+ sensitivity, tighter membrane-binding affinity and longer Ca2+-lipid disassembly kinetics than SYT1.
source: SYT7 has higher Ca2+ sensitivity, tighter membrane-binding affinity and longer Ca2+-lipid disassembly kinetics than SYT1 (Hui et al., 2005; Sugita et al., 2002; Sugita et al., 2001; Voleti et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge about SYT7 biochemical properties, supported by citations.

claim: Mammalian SYT7 has been implicated in SV endocytosis, SV replenishment, SV pool mobility, and DCV fusion and replenishment.
source: Besides asynchronous release and facilitation, mammalian SYT7 has been implicated in SV endocytosis, SV replenishment, SV pool mobility, and DCV fusion and replenishment (Bacaj et al., 2015; Dolai et al., 2016; Durán et al., 2018; Fukuda et al., 2004; Gustavsson et al., 2011; Li et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2014; Schonn et al., 2008; Tsuboi and Fukuda, 2007; Virmani, 2003; Wu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on mammalian SYT7 functions.

claim: SYT7 has been shown to regulate cell migration, lysosomal fusion and membrane repair in non-neuronal cells.
source: SYT7 has also been shown to regulate cell migration, lysosomal fusion and membrane repair in non-neuronal cells (Barzilai-Tutsch et al., 2018; Chakrabarti et al., 2003; Colvin et al., 2010; Czibener et al., 2006; Flannery et al., 2010; Jaiswal et al., 2004; Martinez et al., 2000; Reddy et al., 2001; Zhao et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on SYT7 in non-neuronal cells.

claim: Drosophila SYT7 is 59% identical to human SYT7.
source: Drosophila SYT7 is 59% identical to human SYT7.
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment analysis performed in the study.

claim: The N-terminus encoding the transmembrane domain and linker region has the greatest variability between SYT1 and SYT7 subfamilies and shares only 21% identity.
source: Comparing the SYT1 and SYT7 subfamilies, the N-terminus encoding the transmembrane domain and linker region has the greatest variability and shares only 21% identity.
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment analysis performed in the study.

claim: There is 100% conservation of the negatively charged Ca2+ binding residues in the C2 loops between SYT1 and SYT7.
source: Within the C2 domains, there is 100% conservation of the negatively charged Ca2+ binding residues in the C2 loops.
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment analysis performed in the study.

claim: A polybasic stretch in the C2B domain that mediates Ca2+-independent PI(4,5)P2-lipid interactions is conserved between SYT1 and SYT7.
source: A polybasic stretch in the C2B domain that mediates Ca2+-independent PI(4,5)P2-lipid interactions is also conserved.
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment analysis performed in the study.

claim: Four of the five primary SNARE binding residues are not conserved in Drosophila SYT7.
source: Five key C2B residues (S332, R334, E348, Y391, A455) form the primary interaction site that docks SYT1 onto the SNARE complex (Guan et al., 2017; Zhou et al., 2015). Four of the five primary SNARE binding residues are not conserved in Drosophila SYT7 (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment and structural analysis performed in the study.

claim: Drosophila and mammalian SYT7 contain specific amino acids substitutions at two residues that block SNARE binding and abolish SYT1 function in SV fusion.
source: In addition, Drosophila and mammalian SYT7 contain specific amino acids substitutions at two of these residues that block SNARE binding and abolish SYT1 function in SV fusion (Guan et al., 2017), including C285 (corresponding to Syt1 mutant R334C) and K299 (corresponding to Syt1 mutant E348K).
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment analysis and comparison to prior functional studies, supported by citation.

claim: SYT7 is unlikely to engage the SNARE complex via the primary or secondary C2B interface.
source: As such, SYT7 is unlikely to engage the SNARE complex via the primary or secondary C2B interface, highlighting a key difference in how the proteins regulate membrane trafficking.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the sequence analysis showing lack of conservation of SNARE-binding residues.

claim: Drosophila Syt7 null mutants are viable and fertile with no obvious behavioral defects.
source: Similar to the loss of SYT7 in mice (Maximov et al., 2008), Drosophila Syt7 null mutants are viable and fertile with no obvious behavioral defects.
evidence: This is an observation from the study, with comparison to prior mouse studies via citation.

claim: No significant changes in spontaneous release parameters were identified in Syt7M1 mutants.
source: No significant changes in spontaneous release parameters were identified, as miniature excitatory junctional current (mEJC) amplitude, kinetics and frequency were similar between Syt7M1 mutants, Syt7M1 heterozygotes (Syt7M1/+) and controls (Figure 2A–D).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data presented in Figure 2A-D.

claim: Evoked SV fusion was dramatically enhanced in Syt7M1 single mutants.
source: In contrast to spontaneous release, evoked SV fusion (excitatory evoked junctional current (eEJC)) was dramatically enhanced in Syt7M1 single mutants and elevated to an intermediate level in Syt7M1 heterozygotes (Figure 2E,F; control: 158.33 ± 19.13 nA, n = 9; Syt7M1/+: p<0.05, 233.08 ± 19.16 nA, n = 14; Syt7M1: p<0.005, 262.96 ± 13.01 nA, n = 10).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data presented in Figure 2E,F.

claim: Evoked SV fusion was elevated to an intermediate level in Syt7M1 heterozygotes.
source: In contrast to spontaneous release, evoked SV fusion (excitatory evoked junctional current (eEJC)) was dramatically enhanced in Syt7M1 single mutants and elevated to an intermediate level in Syt7M1 heterozygotes (Figure 2E,F; control: 158.33 ± 19.13 nA, n = 9; Syt7M1/+: p<0.05, 233.08 ± 19.16 nA, n = 14; Syt7M1: p<0.005, 262.96 ± 13.01 nA, n = 10).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data presented in Figure 2E,F.

claim: There was no change in eEJC kinetics in Syt7M1 or Syt7M1/+.
source: Although evoked release was increased ~2 fold, there was no change in eEJC kinetics in Syt7M1 or Syt7M1/+ (Figure 2G,H).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data presented in Figure 2G,H.

claim: eEJC half-width was unaffected in Syt7M1.
source: In addition, eEJC half-width was unaffected (Figure 2I).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data presented in Figure 2I.

claim: Loss of SYT7 increased evoked release regardless of whether quantal content was estimated using eEJC amplitude or eEJC charge.
source: Loss of SYT7 increased evoked release regardless of whether quantal content was estimated using eEJC amplitude (which primarily measures synchronous release, 98% increase, Figure 2J) or eEJC charge (which measures both synchronous and asynchronous release, 128% increase, Figure 2K).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data presented in Figure 2J,K.

claim: The enhanced evoked release in Syt7M1 was observed over a large range of extracellular [Ca2+] spanning from 0.175 to 2 mM.
source: The enhanced evoked release in Syt7M1 was observed over a large range of extracellular [Ca2+] spanning from 0.175 to 2 mM (Figure 2L).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data presented in Figure 2L.

claim: There was no significant difference in the Ca2+ cooperativity of release between control and Syt7M1.
source: Although the Ca2+ response curve shifted leftward over the entire range in Syt7M1, regression analysis revealed no significant difference in the Ca2+ cooperativity of release (control: 2.98 ± 0.17 (n = 7 larvae); Syt7M1: 2.69 ± 0.50 (n = 7 larvae), p=0.53).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of Ca2+ dose-response data in Figure 2L.

claim: SYT7 overexpression resulted in a ~ 2 fold decrease in mEJC frequency.
source: However, SYT7 overexpression resulted in a ~ 2 fold decrease in mEJC frequency (Figure 2C, p<0.05), suggesting elevated levels of SYT7 can reduce spontaneous fusion.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data presented in Figure 3C.

claim: SYT7 overexpression caused a striking reduction in eEJC amplitude and eEJC charge.
source: Unlike the increased evoked release in Syt7M1 and Syt7M1/+ mutants, SYT7 overexpression caused a striking reduction in eEJC amplitude (Figure 3D,E) and eEJC charge (Figure 3F), with only mild effects on SV release kinetics (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data presented in Figure 3D-G.

claim: Overexpression of SYT7 in muscles had no effect on eEJC amplitude or kinetics.
source: To determine if the inhibitory action of SYT7 on SV release is secondary to a presynaptic role, SYT7 was overexpressed postsynaptically using the muscle specific Mhc-GAL4 driver. Overexpression of SYT7 in muscles had no effect on eEJC amplitude or kinetics (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: There was no change in the total number of synaptic boutons in Syt7M1 mutants.
source: There was no change in the total number of synaptic boutons (Figure 4C,F), AZ number defined by BRP puncta (Figure 4D,G), or AZ number per muscle surface area (Figure 4E,H).
evidence: This is supported by immunocytochemistry data presented in Figure 4C-H.

claim: There was no change in AZ number defined by BRP puncta in Syt7M1 mutants.
source: There was no change in the total number of synaptic boutons (Figure 4C,F), AZ number defined by BRP puncta (Figure 4D,G), or AZ number per muscle surface area (Figure 4E,H).
evidence: This is supported by immunocytochemistry data presented in Figure 4C-H.

claim: There was no change in AZ number per muscle surface area in Syt7M1 mutants.
source: There was no change in the total number of synaptic boutons (Figure 4C,F), AZ number defined by BRP puncta (Figure 4D,G), or AZ number per muscle surface area (Figure 4E,H).
evidence: This is supported by immunocytochemistry data presented in Figure 4C-H.

claim: Syt7M1 mutants displayed a 25% decrease in the average volume of individual BRP-labeled T-bars.
source: Although BRP ring structure was intact, Syt7M1 mutants displayed a 25% decrease in the average volume of individual BRP-labeled T-bars (Figure 4J), but no change in the spacing of T-bars relative to each other (Figure 4K).
evidence: This is supported by Airyscan confocal imaging data presented in Figure 4J.

claim: There was no change in the spacing of T-bars relative to each other in Syt7M1 mutants.
source: Although BRP ring structure was intact, Syt7M1 mutants displayed a 25% decrease in the average volume of individual BRP-labeled T-bars (Figure 4J), but no change in the spacing of T-bars relative to each other (Figure 4K).
evidence: This is supported by Airyscan confocal imaging data presented in Figure 4K.

claim: Maximum presynaptic Flou-4 AM fluorescence during the stimulation paradigm was significantly greater in control than in Syt7M1.
source: Maximum presynaptic Flou-4 AM fluorescence during the stimulation paradigm was significantly greater in control than in Syt7M1 (control: 10.7 × 106 ± 1.25 × 106, n = 11 NMJs from eight larvae; Syt7M1: 6.52 × 106 ± 0.75 × 106, n = 9 NMJs from eight larvae, p<0.01, Figure 4L,M).
evidence: This is supported by Fluo-4 AM imaging data presented in Figure 4L,M.

claim: SYT7 does not suppress release by acting as a Ca2+ buffer or a negative regulator of Ca2+ channel function.
source: These data indicate SYT7 does not suppress release by acting as a Ca2+ buffer or a negative regulator of Ca2+ channel function.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that presynaptic Ca2+ influx is reduced in Syt7 mutants.

claim: No change in overall SV density was observed within Syt7M1 boutons.
source: No change in overall SV density was observed within Syt7M1 boutons, indicating SV recycling is largely unperturbed (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data presented in Figure 5B.

claim: There was no change in the length of individual AZs defined by the electron dense synaptic cleft in Syt7M1 mutants.
source: In contrast to the mild decrease in T-bar area (Figure 4J), there was no change in the length of individual AZs defined by the electron dense synaptic cleft (Figure 5C, p=0.93; control: 404 ± 34.5 nm, n = 21 AZs from five larvae; Syt7M1: 409 ± 28.9 nm, n = 29 AZs from five larvae).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data presented in Figure 5C.

claim: No significant change in the number of SVs docked at the AZ plasma membrane was detected in Syt7M1 mutants.
source: No significant change in the number of SVs docked at the AZ plasma membrane was detected (Figure 5D–F), indicating morphological docking defined by EM is not altered in Syt7M1 mutants.
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data presented in Figure 5D-F.

claim: No significant difference in SV distribution was observed in any bin around AZs in Syt7M1 mutants.
source: To quantify SV distribution in the cytoplasm around AZs, SV number was binned into four concentric hemi-circles from 100 to 400 nm radius centered on the T-bar. No significant difference in SV distribution was observed in any bin (Figure 5G,H), indicating the morphological distribution of SVs around T-bars is intact in the absence of SYT7.
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data presented in Figure 5G,H.

claim: Pr distribution was strikingly different between control and Syt7M1, with a greater number of high Pr and fewer low Pr AZs at Syt7M1 NMJs.
source: Similar to controls, AZs formed by single motor neurons in Syt7M1 displayed heterogeneous Pr (Figure 6B). However, Pr distribution was strikingly different between the genotypes, with a greater number of high Pr and fewer low Pr AZs at Syt7M1 NMJs (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by optical quantal imaging data presented in Figure 6B,C.

claim: Syt7M1 NMJs had fewer silent AZs that showed no release (control: 19.9%; Syt7M1: 4.6%).
source: Syt7M1 NMJs also had fewer silent AZs that showed no release (control: 19.9%; Syt7M1: 4.6%).
evidence: This is supported by optical quantal imaging data presented in Figure 6.

claim: Mean Pr was increased 2-fold in Syt7M1 compared to control.
source: Overall, mean Pr was increased 2-fold (Figure 6D, p<0.01; control: 0.063 ± 0.002, n = 1158 AZs; Syt7M1: 0.12 ± 0.004, n = 768 AZs).
evidence: This is supported by optical quantal imaging data presented in Figure 6D.

claim: The maximum AZ Pr in control and Syt7M1 was unchanged (control: 0.61; Syt7M1: 0.63).
source: In contrast, the maximum AZ Pr in the two genotypes was unchanged (Figure 6D, control: 0.61; Syt7M1: 0.63), indicating an upper limit on release strength for single AZs that is similar between controls and Syt7M1.
evidence: This is supported by optical quantal imaging data presented in Figure 6D.

claim: 45.3% of Syt1Null mutants survived from the 1st instar to the pupal stage.
source: Quantification of survival rates demonstrated 45.3% of Syt1Null mutants survived from the 1st instar to the pupal stage, with 44.1% of mutant pupae surviving to adulthood (n = 5 groups with >40 starting animals each).
evidence: This is based on survival rate quantification performed in the study.

claim: 44.1% of Syt1Null mutant pupae survived to adulthood.
source: Quantification of survival rates demonstrated 45.3% of Syt1Null mutants survived from the 1st instar to the pupal stage, with 44.1% of mutant pupae surviving to adulthood (n = 5 groups with >40 starting animals each).
evidence: This is based on survival rate quantification performed in the study.

claim: 5.6% of Syt1Null; Syt7M2 double mutants survived from the 1st instar to the pupal stage.
source: In contrast, 5.6% of Syt1Null; Syt7M2 double mutants (referred to as DoubleNull) survived from the 1st instar to the pupal stage, and 6.6% of mutant pupae survived to adulthood (n = 6 groups with >80 animals each).
evidence: This is based on survival rate quantification performed in the study.

claim: 6.6% of Syt1Null; Syt7M2 double mutant pupae survived to adulthood.
source: In contrast, 5.6% of Syt1Null; Syt7M2 double mutants (referred to as DoubleNull) survived from the 1st instar to the pupal stage, and 6.6% of mutant pupae survived to adulthood (n = 6 groups with >80 animals each).
evidence: This is based on survival rate quantification performed in the study.

claim: No change in spontaneous mEJC amplitude or kinetics was found between Syt1Null and DoubleNull mutants.
source: No change in spontaneous mEJC amplitude or kinetics was found between the two genotypes (Figure 7B), indicating postsynaptic sensitivity, neurotransmitter loading, and fusion pore dynamics were not disrupted by loss of SYT7.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data presented in Figure 7B.

claim: A ~ 2 fold increase in mEJC frequency was observed in the DoubleNull compared to Syt1Null.
source: However, a ~ 2 fold increase in mEJC frequency was observed in the DoubleNull compared to Syt1Null (Figure 7C, p<0.001; Syt1null: 2.99 ± 0.23 Hz, n = 16; DoubleNull: 5.33 ± 0.42 Hz, n = 14), demonstrating loss of both SYTs enhances the already elevated spontaneous release rate found in Syt1Null mutants alone.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data presented in Figure 7C.

claim: Both amplitude and charge transfer were increased ~2 fold in DoubleNull compared to Syt1Null mutants.
source: Measurements of evoked release revealed both amplitude and charge transfer were increased ~2 fold in DoubleNull compared to Syt1Null mutants (Figure 7D–F; eEJC amplitude: p<0.001; Syt1Null: 3.18 ± 0.4 nA, n = 15; DoubleNull: 6.12 ± 0.62 nA, n = 13; eEJC charge: p<0.05; Syt1Null: 33.2 ± 4.4 nA*ms, n = 15; DoubleNull: 52.6 ± 5.8 nA*ms, n = 13).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data presented in Figure 7D-F.

claim: More SVs fused in the first 15 ms following stimulation in DoubleNull compared to Syt1Null.
source: In addition, more SVs fused in the first 15 ms following stimulation (Figure 7G,H), with less SVs available for release later in the response.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data presented in Figure 7G,H.

claim: DoubleNull mutants had a reduced rate of evoked failures following nerve stimulation compared to Syt1Null.
source: DoubleNull mutants also had a reduced rate of evoked failures following nerve stimulation compared to Syt1Null, consistent with an increased probability of SV release (Figure 7I, p<0.01; Syt1Null: 21.1 ± 3.5% failure rate, n = 17; DoubleNull: 7.4 ± 3.4% failure rate, n = 14).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data presented in Figure 7I.

claim: Control and Syt7M1 mutants displayed robust facilitation to paired pulses separated by 10 or 50 ms.
source: Control and Syt7M1 mutants displayed robust facilitation to paired pulses separated by 10 or 50 ms at both Ca2+ concentrations (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data presented in Figure 8D.

claim: A modest reduction in paired-pulse ratio was observed in Syt7M1 at 0.175 Ca2+ compared to control at 0.2 mM Ca2+.
source: A modest reduction in paired-pulse ratio was observed in Syt7M1 at 0.175 Ca2+ compared to control at 0.2 mM Ca2+ (Figure 8E,F, p<0.05; 10 ms interval: 31% decrease; 50 ms interval: 22% decrease).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data presented in Figure 8E,F.

claim: DoubleNull mutants displayed larger facilitating responses during the early phase of stimulation compared to Syt1Null.
source: Similar to the increased quantal content to single action potentials, DoubleNull mutants displayed larger facilitating responses during the early phase of stimulation (Figure 8G–I; cumulative average release for 10 stimuli: Syt1Null (n = 12): 87 ± 7.0 quanta; DoubleNull (n = 13): 109 ± 9.9 quanta; 20 stimuli: Syt1Null: 209 ± 13.8 quanta; DoubleNull: 261 ± 22.6 quanta; 50 stimuli: Syt1Null: 594 ± 34.5 quanta; DoubleNull: 745 ± 56.2 quanta, p<0.03).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data presented in Figure 8G-I.

claim: SV release in Syt7M1 mutants remained elevated over much of the initial stimulation during a 10 Hz train.
source: Both control and Syt7M1 eEJCs depressed during the stimulation train. However, SV release in Syt7M1 mutants remained elevated over much of the initial stimulation (Figure 9A) and the integral of release during the train was greater than controls (Figure 9B), indicating Syt7 nulls have access to more fusogenic SVs.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data presented in Figure 9A,B.

claim: The integral of release during the train was greater in Syt7M1 than controls.
source: Both control and Syt7M1 eEJCs depressed during the stimulation train. However, SV release in Syt7M1 mutants remained elevated over much of the initial stimulation (Figure 9A) and the integral of release during the train was greater than controls (Figure 9B), indicating Syt7 nulls have access to more fusogenic SVs.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data presented in Figure 9B.

claim: SV release rate in Syt7M1 eventually reached the same level as control following depletion of the RRP.
source: SV release rate in Syt7M1 eventually reached the same level as control following depletion of the RRP (Figure 9C, control quantal content: 131.5 ± 10.7, n = 7; Syt7M1 quantal content: 123.1 ± 10.5, n = 8).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data presented in Figure 9C.

claim: SV endocytosis and recycling rate is SYT7-independent at steady-state.
source: We conclude that SV endocytosis and recycling rate is SYT7-independent at steady-state, although Syt7M1 mutants contain a larger RRP available for fusion.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that steady-state release rates are similar between control and Syt7M1.

claim: Syt7M1 mutants took up significantly more FM1-43 dye than controls at low stimulation rates (0.5 Hz).
source: At low stimulation rates (0.5 Hz), Syt7M1 mutants took up significantly more FM1-43 dye than controls (Figure 9D,F), consistent with the increased SV release observed by physiology.
evidence: This is supported by FM1-43 imaging data presented in Figure 9D,F.

claim: No significant difference in FM1-43 uptake was found following high frequency 10 Hz stimulation for 500 stimuli between control and Syt7M1.
source: In contrast, no significant difference in FM1-43 uptake was found following high frequency 10 Hz stimulation for 500 stimuli (Figure 9E,G).
evidence: This is supported by FM1-43 imaging data presented in Figure 9E,G.

claim: No change in FM1-43 release was detected with high [K+] stimulation following 10 Hz loading between control and Syt7M1.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, no change in FM1-43 release was detected with high [K+] stimulation following 10 Hz loading (Figure 9H).
evidence: This is supported by FM1-43 imaging data presented in Figure 9H.

claim: Syt7M1 and Syt7M1/+ displayed an extremely rapid recovery of eEJC amplitude and quantal content during the 2 s interval following termination of the 10 Hz train compared to controls.
source: Remarkably, Syt7M1 and Syt7M1/+ displayed an extremely rapid recovery of eEJC amplitude and quantal content during the 2 s interval following termination of the 10 Hz train compared to controls (Figure 10C).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data presented in Figure 10C.

claim: A similar rapid recovery was observed in Syt7M1 after 2000 stimuli were given at 10 Hz to fully deplete the RRP and normalize release rates to control levels.
source: A similar rapid recovery was observed in Syt7M1 after 2000 stimuli were given at 10 Hz to fully deplete the RRP and normalize release rates to control levels (Figure 10—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data presented in Figure 10—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: The enhanced refilling of the RRP did not require SYT1 function, as DoubleNull mutants also displayed larger eEJCs than Syt1Null alone during the recovery from a 10 Hz stimulation train.
source: The enhanced refilling of the RRP did not require SYT1 function, as DoubleNull mutants also displayed larger eEJCs than Syt1Null alone during the recovery from a 10 Hz stimulation train (Figure 8G).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data presented in Figure 8G.

claim: Presynaptic overexpression of SYT7 greatly limited the ability of SVs to re-enter the RRP following termination of the 10 Hz stimulation train.
source: Presynaptic overexpression of SYT7 had the opposite effect of Syt7 mutants and Syt7/+ heterozygotes, not only reducing eEJC amplitude at 0.5 Hz, but greatly limiting the ability of SVs to re-enter the RRP following termination of the 10 Hz stimulation train (Figure 10—figure supplement 2A-C).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data presented in Figure 10—figure supplement 2A-C.

claim: Syt7M1 mutants displayed a similar fold-enhancement in the recovery of the RRP in the presence of bafilomycin.
source: Syt7M1 mutants displayed a similar fold-enhancement in the recovery of the RRP in the presence of bafilomycin, though the absolute numbers of SVs re-entering the pool decreased following the 2nd 10 Hz stimulation as the number of neurotransmitter-containing SVs declined (Figure 10E,F).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data presented in Figure 10E,F.

claim: The rapid refilling of the RRP can occur from pre-existing SV pools.
source: We conclude that the rapid refilling of the RRP can occur from pre-existing SV pools.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that enhanced RRP refilling persists in the presence of bafilomycin.

claim: The RFP C-terminal fusion did not abolish SYT7 function, as eEJC amplitude in 2 mM Ca2+ was not significantly different between control and SYT7RFP.
source: The RFP C-terminal fusion did not abolish SYT7 function, as eEJC amplitude in 2 mM Ca2+ was not significantly different between control and SYT7RFP (control: 198.9 ± 8.8 nA, n = 14; SYT7RFP, 227 ± 11.3 nA, n = 14, p=0.1).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data comparing control and SYT7RFP.

claim: Western blot analysis with anti-RFP identified a single band at the predicted molecular weight (73kD) of the fusion protein in SYT7RFP animals.
source: Western blot analysis with anti-RFP identified a single band at the predicted molecular weight (73kD) of the fusion protein in SYT7RFP animals (Figure 11B), indicating a single SYT7 isoform is expressed in Drosophila.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data presented in Figure 11B.

claim: A single SYT7 isoform is expressed in Drosophila.
source: Western blot analysis with anti-RFP identified a single band at the predicted molecular weight (73kD) of the fusion protein in SYT7RFP animals (Figure 11B), indicating a single SYT7 isoform is expressed in Drosophila.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation of a single band on western blot.

claim: SYT7RFP was enriched in presynaptic terminals and formed an expansive tubular network near the plasma membrane that extended into the center of the bouton.
source: Immunostaining of 3rd instar larvae with anti-RFP antisera revealed SYT7RFP was enriched in presynaptic terminals and formed an expansive tubular network near the plasma membrane that extended into the center of the bouton (Figure 11C,D).
evidence: This is supported by immunocytochemistry data presented in Figure 11C,D.

claim: Neuronal knockdown of Syt7 with two independent RNAi lines dramatically reduced SYT7RFP on western blots and eliminated expression of SYT7RFP at the NMJ.
source: Neuronal knockdown of Syt7 with two independent RNAi lines (elavC155-GAL4; UAS-Syt7 RNAi) dramatically reduced SYT7RFP on western blots (Figure 11B) and eliminated expression of SYT7RFP at the NMJ (Figure 11—figure supplement 2), indicating the signal is specific to SYT7 and localizes predominantly to the presynaptic compartment.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data in Figure 11B and immunocytochemistry data in Figure 11—figure supplement 2.

claim: The signal is specific to SYT7 and localizes predominantly to the presynaptic compartment.
source: Neuronal knockdown of Syt7 with two independent RNAi lines (elavC155-GAL4; UAS-Syt7 RNAi) dramatically reduced SYT7RFP on western blots (Figure 11B) and eliminated expression of SYT7RFP at the NMJ (Figure 11—figure supplement 2), indicating the signal is specific to SYT7 and localizes predominantly to the presynaptic compartment.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the RNAi knockdown experiments.

claim: The largest overlap of SYT7 was with Dynamin (r = 0.22).
source: Co-localization analysis indicates SYT7 resides on a membrane compartment that does not completely overlap with any protein tested (Figure 12B–L). The largest overlap was with Dynamin (Figure 12B, r = 0.22), a GTPase involved in endocytosis that localizes to the peri-AZ.
evidence: This is supported by co-localization analysis data presented in Figure 12B.

claim: The t-SNARE SYX1 overlapped with a subset of SYT7 immunolabeling near the plasma membrane (r = 0.15).
source: The t-SNARE SYX1 also overlapped with a subset of SYT7 immunolabeling near the plasma membrane (Figure 12C, r = 0.15).
evidence: This is supported by co-localization analysis data presented in Figure 12C.

claim: SYT7 did not co-localize with Reticulon-like 1 (RTLN1, r = 0.01), a peripheral ER marker.
source: Although SYT7's pattern of inter-connectivity within the bouton appeared similar to peripheral ER, it did not co-localize with Reticulon-like 1 (RTLN1, Figure 12D, r = 0.01), a peripheral ER marker.
evidence: This is supported by co-localization analysis data presented in Figure 12D.

claim: SYT7 did not co-localize with SVs (r = −0.17).
source: In addition, SYT7 did not co-localize with SVs (r = −0.17), DCVs labeled with ANF-GFP (r = −0.07), exosomes (r = −0.19), late endosomes (r = −0.29), lysosomes (r = −0.01) or the plasma membrane (anti-HRP, r = −0.06).
evidence: This is supported by co-localization analysis data presented in Figure 12.

claim: SYT7 did not co-localize with DCVs labeled with ANF-GFP (r = −0.07).
source: In addition, SYT7 did not co-localize with SVs (r = −0.17), DCVs labeled with ANF-GFP (r = −0.07), exosomes (r = −0.19), late endosomes (r = −0.29), lysosomes (r = −0.01) or the plasma membrane (anti-HRP, r = −0.06).
evidence: This is supported by co-localization analysis data presented in Figure 12.

claim: SYT7 did not co-localize with exosomes (r = −0.19).
source: In addition, SYT7 did not co-localize with SVs (r = −0.17), DCVs labeled with ANF-GFP (r = −0.07), exosomes (r = −0.19), late endosomes (r = −0.29), lysosomes (r = −0.01) or the plasma membrane (anti-HRP, r = −0.06).
evidence: This is supported by co-localization analysis data presented in Figure 12.

claim: SYT7 did not co-localize with late endosomes (r = −0.29).
source: In addition, SYT7 did not co-localize with SVs (r = −0.17), DCVs labeled with ANF-GFP (r = −0.07), exosomes (r = −0.19), late endosomes (r = −0.29), lysosomes (r = −0.01) or the plasma membrane (anti-HRP, r = −0.06).
evidence: This is supported by co-localization analysis data presented in Figure 12.

claim: SYT7 did not co-localize with lysosomes (r = −0.01).
source: In addition, SYT7 did not co-localize with SVs (r = −0.17), DCVs labeled with ANF-GFP (r = −0.07), exosomes (r = −0.19), late endosomes (r = −0.29), lysosomes (r = −0.01) or the plasma membrane (anti-HRP, r = −0.06).
evidence: This is supported by co-localization analysis data presented in Figure 12.

claim: SYT7 did not co-localize with the plasma membrane (anti-HRP, r = −0.06).
source: In addition, SYT7 did not co-localize with SVs (r = −0.17), DCVs labeled with ANF-GFP (r = −0.07), exosomes (r = −0.19), late endosomes (r = −0.29), lysosomes (r = −0.01) or the plasma membrane (anti-HRP, r = −0.06).
evidence: This is supported by co-localization analysis data presented in Figure 12.

claim: Neither SYT7RFP nor SYT7GFP was enriched at AZs, but instead surrounded BRP.
source: Neither SYT7RFP (Figure 12G, r = −0.11) or SYT7GFP (Figure 11—figure supplement 1B) was enriched at AZs, but instead surrounded BRP as previously described for other peri-AZ proteins.
evidence: This is supported by co-localization analysis data presented in Figure 12G and Figure 11—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Manipulations of RAB5 (early endosomes), RAB7 (late endosomes) or RAB4 and RAB11 (recycling endosomes) did not disrupt the abundance or morphology of the SYT7 tubular network.
source: Manipulations of RAB5 (early endosomes), RAB7 (late endosomes) or RAB4 and RAB11 (recycling endosomes) did not disrupt the abundance or morphology of the SYT7 tubular network (Figure 12—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data presented in Figure 12—figure supplement 2.

claim: No change in the distribution of several compartment markers were found in Syt7M1 mutants, including the early endosomal marker RAB5, the late endosomal/peri-AZ marker RAB11 and the peri-AZ protein Nervous Wreck (NWK).
source: Similarly, no change in the distribution of several compartment markers were found in Syt7M1 mutants, including the early endosomal marker RAB5, the late endosomal/peri-AZ marker RAB11 and the peri-AZ protein Nervous Wreck (NWK) (Figure 12—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data presented in Figure 12—figure supplement 3.

claim: No defect was observed in trans-synaptic transfer of the exosomal protein SYT4 to the postsynaptic compartment in Syt7M1 mutants.
source: In addition, no defect was observed in trans-synaptic transfer of the exosomal protein SYT4 to the postsynaptic compartment, indicating SYT7 does not regulate exosome trafficking as described for several other peri-AZ proteins (Walsh et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data and comparison to prior literature via citation.
